paras: The lynching of Oscar M. Garrett took place early on April 24, 1882, when masked men broke into the Decatur County jail at Greensburg, Indiana, and hanged Garrett from a maple tree in front of it. Garrett had been acquitted weeks earlier of complicity in the murder of a farmer, John M. Walton, and the placard left on his body addressed the Jennings County jury that freed him. Papers across the country noted it as a mob reversing a jury's verdict, and the Indiana State Sentinel called it murder.

John M. Walton, a farmer living near St. Paul, was shot through a window of his house on January 9, 1882. Aaron Frazier, described in the papers as "a negro," was arrested and, according to the Sentinel, confessed to the shooting and implicated Walton's wife, Ellen, and Garrett, whom the paper called her "paramour."

After his acquittal at Vernon on a change of venue, he was rearrested on a charge of burning a house near the Walton residence and lodged at Greensburg in a cell normally used for women, with no extra precautions taken.

At about 2 a.m. the doorbell rang, and when jailer William Toothman answered, masked men seized him and demanded the keys to Garrett's cell. When he refused, they put a rope around his neck upstairs, and one man broke the cell lock with a sledgehammer. Garrett knocked down the first man with a chair but was overpowered, beaten, and dragged by the feet down a flight of stone steps, shouting "I know you" as he fought.

With a rope around his neck he was dragged out of the jail to a maple standing in the street in front of it. A card attached to the body read "Fiat justitia ruat coelum. Gone to meet Jesse. Decatur Sends Greeting to Jennings," printed in capitals. The men left westward, some in two spring wagons, after warning the jailer to stay inside, and Sheriff John W. Stout cut the body down.

The Sentinel's correspondent reported that Garrett's clothing had been torn off, that his head bore wounds "as if made with a knife," and that he was probably dead before he was hung. Mrs. Walton and Frazier, held in the same jail, were not harmed, though the Wheeling dispatch described Frazier crouching "in abject terror."

A coroner's jury found that Garrett died by mob violence at the hands of unknown parties, and Judge Bonner instructed the grand jury to find the perpetrators without regard to expense, and two days later it examined ten or fifteen men from near St. Paul without finding a clue; no report of any arrest or indictment was found.
Mrs. Walton's trial was continued to September, and in that month Frazier pleaded guilty to Walton's murder and was sentenced to life in the penitentiary.

Most papers carried a Times-Star dispatch from Cincinnati giving fifty masked men and a placard reading "This is greeting to the Jennings co. jury," often under headlines such as "Judge Lynch in Indiana." Some headlines and dispatches leaned toward the mob: the Los Angeles Herald titled it "Avenging a Miscarriage of Justice," and the Wheeling Register's report said "outraged justice demanded its victim." Race entered the coverage only through Frazier, whom the wire called "a negro named Frazer," and a Raleigh roundup summed up the case as a man who had "helped a negro to murder a white man."

In Indianapolis, the Sentinel's correspondent wrote that while residents deplored mob law, "they indorse its work." The same paper's editorial page called the hanging "murderous anarchy" and said every man involved was a murderer who should be hanged. An editorial reprinted in Kansas and Indian Territory papers called it the worst of the season's lynchings because the mob "reversed the finding of a jury."
Accounts differ on the hour, from 1:30 to 3 a.m., and on the size of the mob, given as fifty by the wire, twenty-five by a prisoner, near 100 from horse tracks, and ten or twelve in one rumor.

reader.title: Lynching of Oscar M. Garrett
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Masked men took Garrett from the Decatur County jail and hanged him from a tree in front of it (A2, A7, A11).

A masked group of at least twenty-five, by every count, took an acquitted prisoner held on another charge from jail and hanged him (A2, A11); the placard 'Decatur Sends Greeting to Jennings' and local talk that 'justice had to get in its work somewhere' frame it as punishment for the acquittal (A8).
The Times-Star wire (A2), the Indiana State Sentinel's own correspondent with inquest testimony (A7, A8, A11, A12) and a separate Greensburg dispatch (A6) agree on the seizure and hanging.

accounts.gist: Fifty masked men choked the jailer, broke in, hanged O. M. Garrett from a maple ten feet from the jail and left a placard greeting the Jennings County jury; fears were voiced for Frazer and Mrs. Walton.

accounts.label: Indiana State Sentinel correspondent
accounts.gist: A detailed local account from the jailer, a prisoner and inquest witnesses: Garrett fought with a chair, was beaten, dragged by the neck and hanged; his body was stripped and battered, and the correspondent thought him probably dead before he was hung.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death by mob violence; parties unknown.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Times-Star dispatch under headlines such as 'Judge Lynch in Indiana' and 'A Mob's Greeting to a Jury'.
The Wheeling Register dispatch said 'outraged justice demanded its victim' and called Garrett 'the murderer of two men'; the Los Angeles Herald headed it 'Avenging a Miscarriage of Justice'.
The Indiana State Sentinel editorial called the hanging 'murderous anarchy' and every participant a murderer, while its correspondent reported local approval.
A Kansas editorial called it 'the worst case of all' because the mob hanged a man a jury had acquitted.
